items.item: Hashing (Chapter 3) and a BST (Chapter 4) trade the same thing in opposite directions: hashing gives up order for O(1) location, a BST keeps order and pays for it in height risk — stated explicitly as the chapter's turn.

at.step: Hashing answered where a key lives by giving up on order completely. This topic keeps the keys in order instead, and asks what that costs.

items.item: Search and insert are not two separate algorithms; insert is literally a search that doesn't stop when it would otherwise report failure, continuing one more step into empty space.

at.step: Search and insert both walk the same comparison: smaller, go left; bigger, go right. Insert just keeps going until it finds an empty spot.

items.item: A sorted insertion order is not a random or unusual case — it is the single most deterministic order possible, and it is also the exact order that produces the worst-case shape.

at.step: Insert these timestamps in already-sorted order instead of random order. What shape does the tree take?

items.item: The BST property is validated at every single insert along a sorted sequence, yet the resulting shape is the worst one achievable — the property is a constraint on key order, not a constraint on shape or height.

at.step: Same keys, same BST property, wildly different height. One insertion order silently degrades search from fast to slow.

items.item: The two-child delete case is the only genuinely hard case; one- and zero-child deletes are handled by simply relinking around the deleted node, with no successor search needed.

at.step: Deleting a two-child node swaps in its in-order successor — the smallest key bigger than it. No key sits between them, so order never breaks.

items.item: In-order traversal's sorted output is a consequence of the tree's shape, not an operation performed on the output afterward — nothing sorts the result; the recursive left-node-right order already is sorted order.

at.step: Walk left, visit, walk right, every single time. That one rule reads every key back out in sorted order.

items.item: A rotation's O(1) cost and order-preservation are not two separate facts to verify; the second follows directly from the first, since only the specific nodes already related by the rotated edge change parent, never any key's relative position.

This topic deliberately declares no balancing invariant for when to rotate, leaving that decision entirely to the following topics (red-black trees, order-statistic trees) rather than anticipating or duplicating their content.

at.out: AVL trees, splay trees, and treaps' own specific balancing invariants are skipped in the syllabus and not claimed here.

items.item: This topic's own measured heights (17 for random order, 200 for sorted order, on the identical 200-key set) are this topic's own honest measurement, not claimed to match any particular textbook's worked example.
A rotation is named here as the shared primitive every later balancing scheme in this chapter will reuse, without yet attaching any invariant that decides when to apply it.
